lines.cap: **Narrator:** Monday, Period 1. Room 8H. Mr Hargreaves is on mug number seven.
**Mr H:** Reminder: your **playscript** and **reflective commentary** are due at **Period 5**.
**Mei:** Easy! Listen to my opening: "I'm not going," Mia shouted angrily, thinking about last summer. Bracket, pause, unbracket.
**Bracket:** STOP! Did you just read a **stage direction** OUT LOUD?!
**Mei:** Why is a pair of square brackets yelling at me?
**Bracket:** I am **Bracket**, an italicised **stage direction**! Actors **do** me, darling, they never **say** me!
**Clapper:** And cut! Take one: unstageable! How does an actor perform 'thinking about last summer'? Stare aggressively at a calendar?
**Will:** In my theatre, actors weren't even handed the whole play: only **cue scripts** with their own lines and a few cue words!
**Will:** Though we also had no air-conditioning, so Singapore wins.
**Mei:** Current script draft: **one star**. Four periods till deadline.
**Narrator:** All the School's a Stage. Episode five: Exit, Pursued by a Deadline.
**Mr H:** A **script** has **no narrator**. Everything must be **heard** in dialogue or **seen** in action.
**Nib:** Follow the layout conventions, mnemonic **SCRIPT**: **S**cene heading first, giving place and time.
**Nib:** Optional **character list**, or **dramatis personae**, then character names in **CAPITALS** at the left margin with a colon.
**Mr H:** **Remove speech marks** and 'she shouted'. Start a **new line** for every speaker.
**Bracket:** Put stage directions in **italics** when typed, or **brackets** when handwritten, always in the **present tense**!
**Nib:** Mark *Enter*, *Exit*, or **Exeunt** — Latin for 'they go out' when several characters leave.
**Bracket:** My golden rule: **See it? Hear it? Or cut it.** 'She feels guilty' is novel narration — turn it into '(She hides the broken china.)'.
**Mei:** So I basically put '(angrily)' before every single line so the actor gets it?
**Nib:** She said 'basically'. I am leaking. Over-directing strangles actors! Use a short **parenthetical** like '(whispering)' only when tone isn't obvious.
**Will:** My most famous direction is five words: **Exit, pursued by a bear**, from The Winter's Tale, Act 3 Scene 3.
**Will:** Mostly I used **embedded stage directions** inside the speech: Juliet's 'Wilt thou be gone? it is not yet near day' tells us it is dawn!
**Clapper:** Screenwriter's rule of thumb: one formatted page equals roughly **one minute** on stage. Keep it crisp!
**Narrator:** Period 2. The library. The SILENCE PLEASE sign has given up.
**Mr H:** Next trap: making every character sound identical. Each needs a distinct **voice**, or **idiolect**.
**Nib:** Build voice from **vocabulary**, **sentence length**, speech **habits**, and what they refuse to say.
**Will:** Cover the names in Romeo and Juliet: my **Nurse** rambles through warm memories, while **Juliet** speaks in quick, sharp thoughts.
**Kevin:** Ooh! Real talk is messy! Use a **dash** for interruptions, an **ellipsis** for trailing off... and me, a comma, for little hesitations!
**Clapper:** And ban the **exposition dump**! Nobody says, 'As you know, Mother, Father was banished last Tuesday.' Let facts slip out through conflict!
**Mr H:** Know your four speech forms. A **monologue** is a long speech when others are **listening**.
**Will:** A **soliloquy** is spoken **alone on stage**, revealing honest private truth — like Juliet's 'Ancient damnation! O most wicked fiend!' after the Nurse exits.
**Mei:** Or like talking to the documentary camera when Mr H isn't looking.
**Will:** Still a soliloquy with worse lighting.
**Nib:** An **aside** is a brief remark to the audience that others on stage do **not** hear, like Hamlet's 'A little more than kin, and less than kind.'
**Nib:** And **stichomythia**: rapid alternating one-line exchanges, like fencing with words! Hamlet's 'Are you honest?' / 'My lord?' / 'Are you fair?'
**Mei:** Okay, stichomythia is cool. Script writing moves up to **two stars**.
**Narrator:** Break time. Mei has a curry puff and a scene where everyone agrees politely.
**Clapper:** Boring! **Conflict** is the engine of drama: a **want** plus an **obstacle**, either **external** between characters or **internal** inside one mind!
**Mei:** So if a character is hurt, she says, 'I am deeply hurt by your betrayal'?
**Bracket:** Never! Real people say 'Fine.' What lies underneath is **subtext** — the hidden nine-tenths of the iceberg!
**Will:** When the Nurse tells Juliet to marry Paris or 'beshrew' her soul, Juliet answers one word: '**Amen!**' Polite on top; a secret curse underneath!
**Nib:** Add **dramatic irony**: when the **audience knows** about Juliet's sleeping potion, 'Your mother will weep' breaks our hearts.
**Clapper:** Now shape the journey: **arrive late, leave early**! Start right near the conflict, and cut out before the tension drains.
**Mr H:** Climb from **set-up** to **complication**, **escalation**, and a **turning point** where power shifts.
**Will:** Then end on a **cliffhanger**, like Juliet's chilling final line in Act 3 Scene 5: 'If all else fail, myself have power to die.'
**Bracket:** Control **pace**! Short lines and interruptions speed up; a **(Pause.)** or a tiny **(Beat.)** makes silence the loudest thing in the room!
**Nib:** And use **juxtaposition**: placing light chatter right before tragedy makes the drop feel twice as steep.
**Narrator:** Period 3. The school hall. Clapper has claimed the stage.
**Clapper:** **Stagecraft** tells the story visually! Remember: **S**ome **P**eople **C**an't **L**eave **S**ound **B**ehind — **Set, Props, Costume, Lighting, Sound, Blocking**!
**Nib:** Plus two spatial tools: **proxemics** — distance between actors showing closeness or rejection — and **levels**, where height signals **status**.
**Mei:** So if Juliet steps left, I write 'stage left' for the left side I'm looking at?
**Bracket:** Trap! Stage directions use the **actor's view**, facing the audience! **Stage left** is the audience's right.
**Clapper:** **Downstage** is nearest the audience, **upstage** furthest away, and **downstage centre** is the power spot for a soliloquy under a spotlight!
**Mr H:** For your **Shakespeare adaptation**, pick one of three routes: **modernise** the setting, write an offstage **missing scene**, or **flip the viewpoint**.
**Will:** Tell the island through **Caliban's** eyes, echoing 'This island's mine, by Sycorax my mother' — or show **Ophelia** alone with Hamlet's letters!
**Mr H:** Keep the **dramatic core**, echo a real quotation, and stay **consistent** with the play's facts: the Nurse never learns about the potion.
**Will:** And give Caliban swagger. I invented 'swagger', you know.
**Nib:** **Earliest recorded user**, Will. Not the same thing.
**Mei:** Missing scene chosen, blackout ending locked. Up to **three and a half stars**!
**Narrator:** Period 4. Mei finishes her script and writes: 'In my scene, Juliet comes home and hides the potion.'
**Mr H:** Mei. I have just read your script. Never retell your own plot. Tell me **why**.
**Nib:** A **commentary** proves every choice was deliberate! Write in the **first person**: cover **purpose**, **audience**, **intended effect**, and **links to Shakespeare**.
**Nib:** Build each paragraph with **CQTEL** — 'Can Quiet Teens Explain Lines?': **Choice, Quote your own script, Term, Effect, Link**!
**Mei:** Right! **Point** and **Choice**: I used **dramatic irony** to show the silent break in trust between Juliet and the Nurse.
**Mei:** **Evidence** — quoting myself! The Nurse says 'Your mother will weep', while Juliet stands 'very still beneath the veil'.
**Mei:** **Explain**: the audience knows the potion will fake Juliet's death, turning wedding joy into grief and the veil into a shroud.
**Mei:** **Link**: this foreshadows the family mourning Juliet in Act 4 Scene 5, echoing her secret 'Amen!' in Act 3 Scene 5.
**Mr H:** Finish with one honest sentence of **evaluation** — what you'd sharpen in a redraft.
**Mr H:** Self-quotation embedded. Terminology exact. That... will score very well.
**Narrator:** Five minutes to Period 5. Six exam traps before you hand it in.
**Mei:** Hooks first! **SCRIPT** for layout; **See it? Hear it? Or cut it**; **Some People Can't Leave Sound Behind**; and **CQTEL** for commentary!
**Bracket:** One. Never write invisible thoughts like '(remembering last summer)'. If we can't see or hear it, cut it!
**Kevin:** Two. **CAPITALS** and a colon in the margin, **no speech marks**, and stage directions in the **present tense**!
**Nib:** Three. Don't slap '(angrily)' on every line, and give each character a distinct **idiolect**.
**Clapper:** Four. **Stage left** is the **actor's left** facing the crowd — **downstage** is closest to the audience!
**Will:** Five. In an adaptation, stay **consistent** with my play's events — don't tell the Nurse about the potion!
**Mr H:** Six. Never retell your plot in the **commentary**. Quote your own script, name the device, and explain the **intended effect**.
**Narrator:** Period 5. Mei hands it in.
**Mei:** Script writing: **four stars**. Deducting one because I had to analyse myself.
**Bracket:** Bracket, **Exeunt**, pursued by a school bell!
**Mr H:** Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
**Mr H:** Do dialogue lines in a playscript use **speech marks**?
**Bracket:** **No**! Character name in **CAPITALS** with a colon, no speech marks, and stage directions in the **present tense**.
**Mr H:** What do we call the hidden meaning **beneath** what a character says aloud?
**Mei:** **Subtext** — the nine-tenths of the iceberg under the surface.
**Mr H:** Rapid alternating **one-line exchanges** in an argument — what is the technical term?
**Nib:** **Stichomythia**.
**Mr H:** Where is **downstage**, and whose left is **stage left**?
**Clapper:** **Downstage** is nearest the audience, and **stage left** is the **actor's left**!
**Mr H:** In a **reflective commentary**, should you retell your plot or **quote your own script** to explain why?
**Mei:** **Quote your own script**, name the technique, explain the **intended effect**, and link to Shakespeare!
**Mr H:** Brilliant work. Now try the **Script Writing & Commentary** quiz in your English Lab.
**Will:** Wait — did nobody use my bear?
**Clapper:** Save the bear for the sequel, Will. Cut!
